newsitem.title: JAPAN: High-tech sector thrives, defying drop in Nikkei.
newsitem.headline: High-tech sector thrives, defying drop in Nikkei.

text.p: Shares in Japanese high-tech and electrical companies spurted higher on Friday, defying an overall drop in the Tokyo market as investors prowled for bargain-priced shares with good earnings prospects.
Brokers said sentiment was not as bad as overall market indices suggested, citing avid interest in particular sectors.

"Investors, both domestic and foreign, are trawling for issues backed by strong earnings, and the buying is sending some of the issues to record highs," said Haruo Nakaharu, a director of Toyo Securities Co Ltd.

There were rallies by some blue-chip leaders such as Sony Corp, which was up 120 yen at 8,900 at 0449 GMT, but brokers said the spotlight was mainly fixed on cheaper issues in the high tech and electricals sectors.

TDK Corp rose 200 yen to a new record high of 9,000 by the midday break, surpassing Sony, the industry leader, as dealers seeking fast profits accelerated a rise that had been ignited by foreign investors. TDK was at 8,980 at 0500 GMT.
The 225-share Nikkei average, meanwhile, was down 1.74 percent at 17,814.38 points in mid-afternoon trade.
Copier and facsimile maker Ricoh Co Ltd, a laggard stock, added 20 yen to stand at 1,490, the third most actively traded issue on the Tokyo bourse with 5.68 million shares traded.

Shares of Advantest Corp, a semiconductor testing device maker, were up 150 yen at 6,850. Semiconductor trading firm Tokyo Electron Ltd edged up 190 yen to a new high for the year of 4,570 yen in a fifth consecutive day of gains.
Tokyo Ohka Kogyo Co Ltd, which makes photoresists for semiconductors, added 150 yen to trade at 3,300.
Brokers said the buying was supported by hopes that the semiconductor market would improve soon and by the firms' solid earnings.

"Apart from foreign investors, domestic institutional investors are reshuffling their portfolios for the new business year which started on April 1, and some are planning to include the smaller, high-tech shares," a broker at a medium-sized brokerage said.

Brokers said the two-tiered state of the market was likely to continue for a while as investors were still in the process of discerning what issues or sectors would lead the market in the new fiscal year.
The trend could strengthen in the coming months, as firms begin to announce their earnings and provide investors with reasons to buy or sell, brokers said.
"There are some banks whose share prices are down at bargain levels," said Hisao Suzuki, Yamaichi Securities deputy general manager.
"But most participants believe the road to recovery is still long and they may steer clear of the sector and opt for shares such as high-techs with bright business prospects."
